claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are primarily governed by competition between continuous protective scales and rapidly forming non-protective oxides.
Cr and Al are high-oxygen-affinity elements that can form stable, adherent, protective oxide scales.
Mn can form rapidly growing, non-protective oxides during high-temperature oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi.
Mn-dominated oxidation depletes the bulk CrMnFeCoNi alloy of Mn.
Reducing Mn content or mobility while increasing the relative amount of Cr or Al will improve oxidation resistance and preserve mechanical integrity.
Near-equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi is susceptible to predominantly Mn-based, non-protective oxide formation at high temperature.
A continuous, adherent oxide nanolayer acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
Suitable diffusion kinetics allow Cr or Al to form a coherent scale that limits oxygen ingress.
Fast Mn surface oxidation produces non-protective scales that compromise material integrity.
The balance between protective and non-protective oxidation pathways determines the overall oxidation rate.
Variants with less Mn or more Cr or Al will have lower mass gain and slower oxidation than near-equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi.
Variants with less Mn or more Cr or Al will form a stable protective oxide scale detectable by XRD and surface microscopy.
The higher-Mn baseline will undergo accelerated deterioration of mechanical integrity.
The proposed behavior is expected to apply from 600 to 900 °C in air for multiprincipal-element alloys with similar constituents and diffusion characteristics.
The hypothesis may not apply when scale spallation caused by thermal cycling or other oxidation mechanisms dominate.
Oxidation kinetics and elemental depletion can vary with processing history and microstructural state.
High-temperature XRD, mass-gain measurements, and post-test microscopy can characterize oxidation kinetics, oxide phases, and scale morphology.
A lack of statistically significant changes in oxidation kinetics, protective-scale formation, and mechanical retention after changing Mn/Cr or Mn/Al ratios would falsify the proposed mechanism.
